FOURTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, 
present this Fourth Report of the Committee on the status of Mini Steel Plants. 
2. The Committee on Industry deals with the subjects falling within the jurisdiction of 
the Ministries of Industry, Steel and Mines. 
3. The Committee at its meeting held on 15th June, 1993 identified 'Mini Steel Plants -
their status' as one of the subjects relating to the Ministry of Steel for its indepth study and 
report. The Committee directed the Secretariat to obtain a note on the subject for its 
consideration. 
4. The Committee held a general discussion on the existing status of Mini Steel Plants in 
the country on Monday, the 28th June, 1993 in the light of the note furnished by the 
Ministry. The Committee finalised a questionnaire for further clarifications by the Ministry 
on the subject. 
5. The Committee also heard the oral evidence of the Secretary of the Ministry on the 
subject on the 29th September, 1993. 
6. The Committee considered the subject in three sittings and considered and adopted 
the Report at its sitting held on 20th December, 1993. 
7.1 In the note submitted to the Committee, the Ministry informed that the term "Mini 
Steel Plant" generally refers to electric arc furnac e unit where melting scrap is reheated and 
refined to produce steel ingots/billets. During the seventies in view of the indigenous 
availability of steel melting scrap , units were allowed to produce mild steel ignots to meet 
the demand of structural steel for construction purposes. At present, there are 177 Mini 
Steel Plants having a total installed capacity of about 7.3 million tonnes of crude steel as per 
the following details:-

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Forty-Second Report 
on the coal India (Regulation ofTransfers and Validation) Bill, 1995. 
2. The Coal India (Regulation of Transfers and Validation) Bill, 1995 was introduced in 
Rajya Sabha on the 141h February, 1995 and was referred * to the Committee on Industry by the 
Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 2nd February, 2000 under Rule 270 (b) of the Rules of 
procedure and Conduct of Business in Rajya Sabha for examination and report thereon. 
3. The Committee in its meeting held on 15th May, 2000 took oral evidence of Secretary of 
Ministry of Coal and Joint Secretary & Legislative Counsel of Ministry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs ( Legislative Department). In Order to take stock of legal issues involved in the 
Bill, the Committee again heard Joint Secretary & Legislative Counsel of the Ministry of Law, 
Justice and Company Affairs on 25th May, 2000. For further clarification, the Committee heard 
the .Secretary ofMinistry of Coal and Ministry Law, Justice and Company Affairs (Legislative 
Department) on 22nd June, 2000. The Committee also took up the clause-by-clause consideration 
of the Bill in the said meeting. 
4. The Committee wishes to thank the representatives of the Ministry of Coal and 
Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs ( Legislative Department) for appearing before the 
Committee for oral evidence and placing their considered views before the Committee. The 
Committee also wishes to thank the Ministry of Coal and the Ministry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs (Legislative Department) for furnishing the replies to the questionnaire and the 
points raised during the course of oral evidence. 
5. The Committee considered and adopted the report on the Bill in its meeting held on 19th 
July, 2000. 
6. A note of dissent given by Shri Jibon Roy, M.P. and Shri Sunil Khan, M.P. is appended 
to the report as Annexure-!.

L the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry. having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Forty-third Report on 
the Credit Flow to Small scale Industries. Taking into account the significance of Small Scale 
Sector it was decided in the Committee's meeting held on 25th September, 2000 that the 
Committee should assess the Credit Flow to the Sector in the aftermath of the policy announced 
by the Hon'ble Prime Minister in the First National Conference of SSI Sector on the 30th August, 
2000. 
2. The Committee at its meeting held on 25th September, 2000, inter-alia examined the 
background note on the Credit Flow to SSI sector furnished by the Ministry of SSI and A&RI 
and thereafter, decided to have interaction with officials of the Ministry of Small Scale 
Industries and Agro & Rural Industries, RBI!Banks/Financial Institutions/KVIC and 
representatives of SSI Association and NGOs to assess the impact of the policy/package on the 
SSI units. 
3. The Committee in its next meeting held on 4th October, 2000 decided to undertake a 
visit to Mumbai from gth to II th October, 2000 to take stock of the ground realities pertaining to 
credit facilities being extended to SSI sector by the Banks and Financial Institutions. 
4. The Report has been prepared on the basis of the background note furnished by the 
Ministry of SSI and A&RI and discussions held in three days meeting in Mumbai with the 
representatives of SSI and NGO and officials the Ministry of SSI and A&RI and RBI/Banks 
and Financial Institutions. On behalf of the Committee I wish to thank all the representatives and 
officials who appeared before the Committee and·· placed their considered views. The 
Committee, while appreciating the concern of the Government to SSI Sector, hopes that the 
Government will implement the recommendations made in the present report in order to ensure 
the continued credit flow to SSI sector. 
5. The Committee in its meeting held on 18th December, 2000 considered and adopted 
the Report.

machine tool industry, heavy electrical industry, industrial machinery and auto-industry. The Industries covered by this
Department provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport.
They also cater to the requirements of equipments for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers,
refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, textiles, paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for development of
a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gear boxes.
It is  also  vested with the administrative charge of 48 Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).

these policies.

growth of small and tiny enterprises, including the coir industries. The Ministry also coordinates with other
Ministries/Departments on behalf the Small Scale Industries (SSI) sector.
 
1.3       Implementation of   policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services
to small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organisation
(SIDO), statutory bodies/other organizations like Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) and Coir Board; a
Public Sector Undertaking – National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC); and three training institutes – National
Institute of Small Industry Extension Training  (NISIET), Hyderabad; National Institute for Entrepreneurship and Small
Business Development (NIESBUD), New Delhi and Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship (IIE), Guwahati.

2. The Committee in its sitting held on 28th June , 1993 considered a note receiv ed from the 
Ministry of Steel on Sponge Iron and decjded to send a questionnaire to the Ministr y on the 
subject for their replies. In its sitting held on 29th September , 1993, the Committe e heard the 
views of the Secretary of the Ministry of Steel by way of clarifications to the repl ies sent by the 
Ministry to the said questionnaire. 
3. The Committee considered in depth the problems prevailing in sponge iron industr y and 
Government's efforts to protect its interests. The Committee had deliberations on the overall 
present scenario with a view to project the possible ways in salvaging the sponge Iron Indust ries. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the report at its sitting held on the lOth February. 
1994. 
5. Based on the papers and other relevant material on the subject and also the evidence of 
the Secretary, the Committee had noted the following picture of the Sponge Iron indu stry in the 
country. 
5.1 Sponge iron is a partial substitute for steel melting Scrap. It is a met allic product 
produced by direct induction of high grade iron ore or pellets in the solid stat e i.e. without the 
material going into the liquid phase as in the blast furnace. It is also known as Direct Reduced 
Iron (DRI) or Hot Briquetted Iron (HBI). This reduction of iron ore can be achieved by using 
either carbon bearing material such as non-coking coal or a suitable redu cing gas produced by 
reforming of natural gas. On the other hand sponge iron can also be used in the integrated steel 
plants to replace steel melting scrap to some extent as a coolant in the LD convertors and as a 
part of the change mix in the basic oxygen furnace and open hearth furnace. 
5.2 Non-coking coal and natural gas are the two main ingredients in spong e iron technology. 
Earlier the technology was limited upto use. of non-coking coal but with the technological 
innovation gas based sponge iron plants have also been set up. While coal based technology 
involves reduction of iron ore in a rotary kiln using non-coking coal as a reduct ant, gas based one 
uses Hydrogen or Carbon Mono Oxide or a mixture of both as reductant s. Gas based sponge iron 
manufacturing process requires high-grade iron ore with around 65%. At present non-coking coal 
is imported for sponge iron industry. Less availability of high grade of iron ore and Jack of

NATIONAL ALUMINIUM COMPANY LTD. (NALCO)
 
1.         Brief   Background
1.1       The  National Aluminium Company Ltd. (NALCO)  was incorporated on 7
th January, 1981 as the second public
sector company in the Aluminium Sector with a view to exploit a part of the large deposits of bauxite discovered in the
east coast. Nalco operates   bauxite mines  at panchpatmali in district Koraput (Orissa).  It runs a  0.8  million tonnes per
Annum  alumina refinery at   Damanjodi in Koraput  District, and  230000  tonnes per  Annum  Aluminium   Smelter  at
Angul  in Orissa.  The authorised capital of the company  has been reduced    from Rs. 1288.62  crores to  Rs.644.31
crores after the approval  of the  Cabinet.   The Government of India  holds  87.15% of equity  in Nalco, the balance

w.e.f. 1st September, 2001. The main function of the Ministry is to formulate policy measures for the growth of rural
industries for achieving rapid increase in gainful employment and balanced regional growth  which are among the main
objectives underlying the strategy of industrialization in the country. It also supervises and coordinates the activities of
different promotional agencies operating at the Central and State Level.

organisations, Trade Marks Attorneys, Legal practitioners and organisations conne~ted with

          I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this Ninetieth Report on Sickness in SSI Sector in the city of Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh.
2.       The Committee, in this context, heard the oral evidence of SSI Associations on 4th June, 2002.

August 9, 2002
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
                                                                      Chairman,
              Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry.
REPORT
BACKGROUND
          Situated on the banks of the river Ganga, Kanpur stands as one of North India's major industrial centres with its
own historical, religious and commercial importance. The city, which was once described as Manchester of the East, is
one of the biggest producers of textile and leather products in Uttar Pradesh. These are exported in bulk from here.
About 50 tonnes of air cargo is generated from leather products only. Apart from leather and textile industries, fertilizer,
chemicals, two wheelers, soaps, pan masala, hosiery and engineering industries are also operating in the city.
1.1     The city hosts the world famous Lal Imli woollen factory, which was once the pride of the State. Besides, many
big companies such as LML Ltd., Kothari Products, Coca Cola, Pepsi, Duncans Industries Ltd. (Fertilizer factory),
Rotomac, Nerolac, Hindustan Lever, Ashok Masale, Goldie Spices, Mirza Tanners, Super House, BIC, NTC, GCMMF
(Amul) etc. have their offices/plants at Kanpur. The stockyards of HAL and SAIL are also located in the city. A large
number of ordnance factories and defence establishments such as DMSRDE, Small Arms Factory, Field Gun Factory
and Parachute Factory are also located in Kanpur. Gas Authority of India Ltd., NTPC, and perfume industries of
Kannauj are very close to Kanpur. A Software Technology Park is also being developed here. The city also hosts the
offices of the Directorate of Industries and Directorate of Handloom to look after these industries.

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER

COIR INDUSTRY -AN OVERVIEW
 
1.0     Coconut cultivation in India is concentrated in Kerala, which accounts for 48.63 per cent of the total production. Historically, the coir
industry took root in Kerala because of the availability of skilled labour and natural facilities of retting of coconut husk.
 
1.1     The development of the coir industry has been in areas where there is concentration of coconut cultivation and availability of coconut husk.
The coir industry is of great importance to Kerala, where it is second only to agriculture as a source of employment. With the expansion of
coconut cultivation and the concerted efforts of the Coir Board and the respective State Governments, the coir industry is coming up in Tamil
Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal and Assam. Kerala is the largest producer of coconuts and its contribution is as much as
50.5 per cent of total production.
 
1.2     Indian coir is exquisite live-in style, hygiene products of traditional and modern design consisting of handmade and machinemade
materials. It is helping a million disadvantaged women to earn their livelihood. Coconut husk is a natural product from a renewable source.

obligations and mutual responsibilities of both the parties are clearly specified indicating the intensions and the objectives to be achieved.

was also envisaged through the system to provide clarity of goals and objectives to be achieved.

CHAPTER-I
INTRODUCTION
1.1   At the time of India’s Independence in 1947, the country had been facing a plethora of problems, which needed to be
tackled in a planned and methodical manner. Primarily, our country being an agrarian economy had negligible industrial
base, low level of savings, inadequate investment with virtually no infrastructural facilities. A large population was below
poverty line and inequalities prevailed in income, levels of employment coupled with lack of trained manpower, which led to
regional imbalances.
1.2   In order to attain the industrial growth, a big initiative was needed from the Government as the private sector had neither
the necessary resources in terms of funds, managerial and scientific skills nor the will to undertake risks involved in large
long gestation investment. In view of the wide range of problems faced by the country on its economic, social and strategic
fronts, it became a necessity to deploy the public sector as an instrument for self-reliant economic growth to overcome the
industrial backwardness. In addition, the adoption of Indian constitution also identified two major National missions, namely
needing self reliance and social justice in the chapter IVof the Constitution.

6.01 The Performance Budget of the Ministry of Mines for the year 1994-95 states that the Ministry is 
primarily responsible for the regulation and development of the mineral sector including the mining and 
metallurgy of all non ferrous metals both in private and public sectors but excluding Natural Gas , Petroleum 
coal and Atomic minerals. Mmeral resources are national assets. Conservation and planned exploitation of 
minerals are therefore, of prime importance to the national economy. Besides providing the basic inputs to 
domestic industry the mineral sector accounts for sizeable exports and foreign exchange earni ngs. Having 
regard to the extent and variety of mineral resources in the country there is great potential for rapid growth 
of this sector. It is the onus of the. Ministry of the Mines to develop this sector with utmost care and caution 
to enable this sector to compete with the contemporary globalisation in the internatio nal area. But the 
Committee finds that the entire mines and minerals sector is in doldrums. Large number of mines have either

1.1       The commitments and mutual responsibilities of the Government and the PSUs are clearly defined in the MoU

CHAPTER–I
LIQUIDATED DAMAGES – THE CONCEPT
            In a supply contract if there is a delay beyond the contractual delivery period in execution of supply, services,
erection and commissioning, the consignee may end up suffering actual or potential losses. Direct losses arising out of
the delay actual in nature that can be directly quantified like debt servicing etc. Potential losses are indirect losses like
opportunity costs, cost overrun of the project, time overrun of the project leading to inflation of project cost etc. The
losses tantamount to the damages suffered by the consignee and quantified unit of these damages are known as
Liquidated Damages.
2.         As per the standard terms of conditions of contracts internationally acclaimed the amount of liquidated damages
is generally ½% of the total value of the contract for every week of delay in supplies or other performance of the
contract plus any cost escalation that has taken place on account of any increase in taxes or imposition of fresh taxes, or
cost escalation of any raw material on account of this during the period of delay, cost escalation of labour due to any
new wage agreement, or imposition of any statutory conditions. However, the supplier will be entitled to any decrease in
cost on the above account of remission of taxes or withdrawal of taxes during the said period between

protection of Small Scale Industries. It also monitors the implementation of these policies.
1.2     Ministry of SSI designs and implements the policies through its field organizations for promotion and growth of
small enterprises. The Ministry also coordinates with other Ministries/Departments on behalf of the Small Scale
Industries (SSI) sector.
1.3     Implementation of policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services to
small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organization
(SIDO).
1.4     The Indian economy has experienced profound changes and sustained growth in the last five decades. Industry
sector, by building core strength of the economy, has acted as an engine of growth. The Small Scale Industries (SSI)
sector has also contributed significantly in process of growth and has emerged as a vibrant partner. The importance of
the sector can be well assessed in terms of its contribution to the socio-economic objectives of growth in generation of
employment, output, exports.

CHAPTER - I 
MOU SYSTEM 
1.         The Memorandum of Undertaking (MOU)  is a negotia ted document between the Government, acting as the owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific
PSE. It contain the intentions, obligations and mutual responsib ilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MOU makes an at tempt to move the management of PSEs
from management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.  
OBJECTIVES OF THE MOU SYSTEM  
1.1       The objectives of the MOU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy and accountability of the management; to remove the
fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise  to pursue through clearly laid down performance targets   in the  MOU and to enable the evaluation of managerial
performance through objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to stimulate improved performance.

INTRODUCTION

been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Hundred and Thirty-first Report on the "The 
Constraints in Industrial Development of North Eastern Region".
 
2.      The Sub-Committee for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises was constituted on the
6th January, 2003. The Sub-Committee has been examining the problems of the PSUs in the NER fo
r
quite some time. The Sub-Committee has deliberated el aborately on various problems being faced by the
industries in its 58th Report. Since there was no head way on the recommendations contained in the
report, the Sub-Committee took up the issues again with various Ministries/Departments connected with
the development of the NER.
 
3.      The report is based on the deliberations of the meetings held with various the 
Ministries/Departments. The Committee heard the oral evidence of representatives of various Ministries 
at New Delhi on 4th February, 24th June and 28th November, 2002, and 22nd April, 23rd July, 7th

I, the Chairman, Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry , 
having been authorised by the Committee, present this Fourteenth Report of the Committee 
on the Demands for Grants for 1995-96 of the Ministry of Steel. 
2. The Committee started examination of Ministry's demands by seeking views of the 
representatives of Chambers of Commerce such as FICCI and the CII on the performance of 
the steel sector and the impact of the recent budget proposals relating to Ministry of Steel. 
The Committee also heard the views of representatives of Central trade unions in the same 
context. 
3. At its subsequent meeting held on the 7th April, 1995, the Committee heard oral 
evidence tendered by the Secretary. Ministry of Steel on the Performance Budget for 1995-
96 in connection with the Dema!lds for Grants of the Ministry. 
4. The Committee eonsidered the Ministry's budgetary proposals in three sittings and 
adopted the report at its sittin~ held on the 28th April, 1995. 
S. The Committee was given to understand that the total demand of ~inistry as per 
Demand No. 75 for 1995-96 is to the tune of Rs. 294.46 crore out of which Rs. 284.50 crore 
is for the Plan sector and remaining Rs. 9.96 crore have been allocated to non-plan 
activities. 
6. Taking into account the documents and other material made available to it and the oral 
evidence tendered before it by the representatives of industry. trade unions and the Ministry 
of Steel, the Committee would like to make the following recommendations and suggestions: 
6.01 The Committee is constrained to make one preliminary observation. A perusal of the 
budgetary allocations for the Ministry · of Steel for the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96 
would suggest that the allocations are declining steadily over the years. Were the factor of 
inflation to be taken into account, the real content of the outlay proposed for the Ministry 
would appear to be declining at an. even sharper gradient. True, in the ambience of 
liberalisation, the authorities could be influenced by the judgement that the role of the 
government in propelling -industrial growth is going to be progressively less and less from 
now on, justifying cutbacks in the outlays for hithertocrucially important ministries, such as

LEVEL  PLAYING  FIELD  FOR
THE  INDIAN  CAPITAL  GOODS  INDUSTRY
 
CHAPTER - I
IMPACT  OF  FISCAL  POLICY  AND  EXIM POLICY  ON  CAPITAL  GOODS  INDUSTRIES
        In early eighties, when India's economy was on an uptrend, there was need for investment in the infrastructure sector.
Investment from within India was not forthcoming mainly because of higher rate of interest and private sector risk aversions.
Investment during those years was mainly from multilateral/bilateral funding agencies. For judicious usage of these funds, the
projects were established under International Competitive Bidding procedures. Indian companies were also eligible to participate
in the bidding procedure. Overseas suppliers could enjoy soft export financing from their exim banking and other export benefits
prevailing in those countries. The Indian companies were also extended the duty free raw material imports and refund of excise
duty on their finished goods to have a level playing field. Supplies to such projects were termed as Deemed Exports.
        As a part of the commitment given to WTO, the peak rate of customs duty was to be brought down to a level agreed with
WTO in a time bound matter and accordingly the rate of customs duty for the project was also reduced gradually. Project import

         The Department of Public Enterprises acts as a nodal agency for all central PSEs and assists in policy formulation
pertaining to the role of PSEs in the economy as also in laying down the policy guidelines on the performance improvement
and evaluation, financial accounting, personnel management and in related areas. It also collects, evaluates and maintains
information on several areas in respect of PSEs. DPE also provides an interface between the administrative Ministries and the
PSEs.
2.      The important role and tasks of the Department are listed below:
(i)     General policy relating to Public Sector.
(ii)     Matters relating to issue of Presidential Directives and guidelines to Public Sector Enterprises.
(iii)    Formulation of policy guidelines pertaining to Public Sector Enterprises in areas like performance improvement
and evaluation, financial management, personnel management, board structures, wage settlement, training,
industrial relation, vigilance, performance appraisal, etc.
(iv)    Matters relating to reservation of posts in the public sector enterprises for certain classes of citizens.

REPORT
          The Agro and Rural Industries Sector has been envisaged as an important avenue for creation of employment in
the rural non-farm sector for the balanced economic growth of the country. The importance of this sector lies in the fact
that it seeks to establish village industries at low cost based on the local raw materials, skills and technology for
providing employment opportunities to the local population and artisans who have been traditionally engaged in village
level economic activities. The main contribution of ARI sector to the National Economy has been in terms of production
and employment generation through setting up of village industries in the rural and semi-urban areas. Over the past five
decades, there has been a big growth in Village Industries (VI) Sector in terms of production and employment.

REPORT
          The Small Scale Industries (SSI) Sector is a vibrant segment of the Indian economy contributing over 39% of the
manufacturing sector output and 34 per cent of the nation’s exports and providing employment to over 270 lakh persons
through more than 115 lakh units, which are spread both in rural and urban areas across the country. The major
contribution of the SSI sector lies in creation of employment opportunities at lower capital cost. While one unit of
employment requires investment of  Rs. 0.72 lakh in SSI sector, the same is as high as Rs. 5 lakh in the large units.
During 2003-04, the SSI sector registered a growth rate of 7.6 per cent as against a growth rate of 6.9 per cent for the
overall industrial sector. The SSI sector contributed 6.81 per cent towards GDP in 2002-03, while the contribution of
manufacturing sector (including SSI) to GDP was around 25 per cent.

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Sixtieth Report on Tax proposals affecting the various segments of
Industries.
2.      The Committee in its meeting held on 28th March, 2005 interacted with the representatives of Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises, Ministry of SSI and SSI Associations like PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry,
FISME, Laghu Udyog Bharti, Indian Plasticizers Manufactures Association (IPMA), Federation of Association of SSI
of India (FASSII), Indian Council of Small Industries (ICSI), Federation of Tiny and Small Industries of India (FTSII),
Indian Paint and Coating Association (IPCA) etc. on the Demands for Grants (2005-06) pertaining to the Ministries of
SSI, ARI and Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises and the impact of Budget proposals affecting the industries. The
Committee in its meeting held on 29th March, 2005 also interacted with the representatives of SIAM, ACMA, ARAI on
the issue of the concerns of auto sector regarding tax proposals in the Budget. After considering the grievances of the
SSI Associations and the representatives of the auto sector and the views of the respective Ministries, the Committee
decided to interact with the Secretary, the Department of Revenue and the Chairman, CBEC in the presence of the SSI
Associations and the representatives of the auto sector to have clarifications regarding the Tax proposal across the
board.
3.      The Committee, therefore, as the fallout of its budgetary exercise for the year        2005-06, interacted on the 12
th
April, 2005 with the representatives of various organizations in the presence of Secretary, Department of Revenue and
Chairman, Central Board for Custom and Excise on the issue of Tax proposals affecting various     segments of
industries. After the detailed discussion, the Committee decided to present a separate Report on “Tax proposals
affecting the various segments of Industries”, addressing various issues brought out by the industrial associations before
the Committee for their redressal.
4.      The Committee in its meeting held on 21st April, 2005 considered and adopted the Report.

sector for the balanced economic growth of the country. The ARI sector seeks to establish village industries at low cost
based on the local raw materials, skills and technology for providing employment opportunities to the local population
and artisans who have been traditionally engaged in village level economic activities.
1.2    The Ministry acts as a nodal agency for promotion and development of agro and rural industries in small towns
and rural areas. The Charter for the Ministry is as follows:-
            1.Coordination of the development of village and cottage industries, and tiny/micro
enterprises in both urban and rural areas.
            2.Coordination of matters relating to all rural industries.
            3.Coir Industries. 
            4.The Coir Board.
            5.Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY).
            6.Khadi and Village Industries Commission.
1.3    The Ministry guides and coordinates with the implementing agencies to ensure development and achievement as
per the set mandate. The Ministry has a multi-pronged role to play in the quality implementation of policies,
programmes and schemes. In the role of a policy maker, the Ministry collects, collates and derives inferences, which act
as critical inputs to further policy formulation/amendments. In the role of an advocate, the Ministry advocates and puts
up ‘felt needs’ of the stakeholders involved in the sector as a whole. In the role of a facilitator, the Ministry facilitates,
coordinates and supports its field agencies in implementing the programmes and schemes both quantitatively and
qualitatively.

Report
 
1.      The Committee took up the issue pertaining to unlocking of surplus assets of the CPSEs to generate resources for their revival
and the status of ancillary units of such CPSEs. In the process of its examination the Committee took up the issue of HMT Ltd.  The
Committee interacted with the management of the HMT Ltd., representatives of Department of Heavy Industries, State Government
of Karnataka and those of the ancillary associations during its visit to Bangalore on 14
th November 2005 at Bengalore and on 21 st

1.0.      Introduction
1.1       The Agro and Rural Industries Sector which falls within the mandate of the Ministry of Agro and Rural
Industries has been envisaged as an important avenue for  employment in the rural non-farm sector for the balanced
economic growth of the country.  The Agro and Rural Industries Sector seeks to establish village industries at low cost
based on the local raw materials, skills and technology for providing employment opportunities to the local population
and artisans who have been traditionally engaged in village level economic activities. The main contribution of ARI
sector to the national economy has been in terms of production and employment generation through setting up of village
industries in the rural and semi-urban areas. The Ministry of ARI has informed the Committee  that  over the past five
decades, there has been a big growth in Village Industries (VI) Sector in terms of production and employment. While in
the year 1955-56, the production in terms of value under village industries was at the level of Rs.10.93 crore, the same
has gone up to Rs.10458.89 crore in 2004-05 and Rs.8778.96 crore in 2005-06 (up to January 2006). Similarly,

1.0       Introduction
 
1.1       In most developed and developing countries of the world such as the USA, France, Germany, China, South Korea, Malaysia and
Thailand, small and medium enterprises are not treated as separate entities but are viewed as one sector in need of almost similar policy
interventions and legal framework. It is only in our country that we have all along targeted small enterprises, especially small scale industries
as a special sector in exclusion of the medium enterprises whose existence we do not recognize neither legally nor other wise.  
 
1.2       Small Scale Industry however, continues to be  defined as an industrial undertaking in which the investment in fixed assets in plant &
machinery, whether held on ownership terms or on lease , or by hire-purchase, does not exceed rupees  one crore. It inter-alia includes, tiny
(micro) enterprises having investment in plant and machinery not exceeding Rs.25 lakh, and  Small Scale Service & Business (industry
related) Enterprises (SSSBE ) with investment in fixed assets, excluding land & building, upto rupees 10 lacs. However, to enhance their
competitiveness both in domestic and global markets by facilitating technological upgradation and adoption of international quality standards,
the investment ceiling in 140  High-Tech And Export Oriented items  and drugs and pharmaceutical sector as a whole,   has been raised from
Rs. 1 crore to Rs.5 crore.
 
1.3       Various sectors and sub-sectors of the SSI are Ancillary Industrial Undertakings, High-Tech And Export Oriented Units, Tiny

2.      Department also administers two national level Institutes namely Fluid Control Research Institute at Palakkad and Automotive Research Association of India, Pune which cater to the needs of flow and
automotive Industry. This Department is also implementing a project on ‘National Automotive Testing and R&D infrastructure Project (NATRIP) through the NATIS, a society set up for this purpose.
 
3.

anticipated overall loss for the year 2005-06 would be Rs. 373.45 crores.

REPORT
 
1.
                  The Committee while assessing the Annual Report of the Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises, Department of Public Enterprises
(DPE) also undertook the examination of the policy of ‘Professionalisation’ of the Boards of the Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs). 
 
2.
                  The Committee was informed by the Ministry of HI & PE that “the PSEs need to be restructured in the new liberalized regime to make them
competitive.”  In a query regarding the viable alternative to the privatization of PSEs.  The Committee was informed by the Ministry that alongwith
other factors like greater functional autonomy, Professionalisation of Boards of PSEs could provide a viable alternative to the privatization. 
 
3.
                  The Committee was also informed that the policy of Professionalisation of Boards was designed “to distance them (PSEs), to the extent possible
from administrative Ministries.”  To this objective the known expert independent Directors were included in the Boards of PSEs.  It was envisaged by
the Government that a Board managed company should be able to take prompt decision and facilitate the implementation.
 
4.
                  The Committee was informed by the DPE that emphasis was laid on inclusion of such persons from outside into the Boards who had experience
in the industry or academics or research in the relevant fields. The policy advocated that measures were required to be taken to make these enterprises
more growth oriented and technically dynamic which was not possible without inducting professionals on the Board of Directors. The non-official
Directors to be inducted on the Board were to be drawn from the public men, technocrats, management experts and consultants and professional
managers in industry and trade with a high degree of proven ability.

1.0       INTRODUCTION
 
1.1       The small scale industries (SSI) sector constitute one of the vibrant sectors of the Indian economy in terms of
employment generation; the strong entrepreneurial base it helps to create and; its share in industrial production and
exports.  The Ministry of SSI designs policies, programmes , projects and schemes in consultation with its organizations
and various stakeholders and monitors their implementation with a view to assisting   the promotion and growth of small
scale industries. The Ministry also performs the function of policy advocacy on behalf of the SSI sector with other
Ministries/Departments of the Central Government and the State and Union Territories.  Taking into account the high
potential for growth in the SSI sector in terms of output, employment and exports, the role of the Ministry of Small
Scale Industries is to strengthen the SSI sector, to enable it to remain competitive in market-led economy and generate
additional employment opportunities. For achieving these objectives, the endeavor of the Ministry is to provide the SSI
sector proper and timely inputs like:
 
(i)
               adequate credit from financial institutions/banks;
(ii)             funds for technology upgradation and modernization;
(iii)            adequate infrastructural facilities;
(iv)           modern testing facilities and quality certification laboratories;
(v)             modern management practices and skill upgradation through advanced training    facilities;
(vi)           marketing assistance; and
(vii)          level playing field at par with the large industries sector.

1.         Tyre Industry was delicensed  in the year 1989.  There are 43 tyre companies in India.  MRF, Apollo, JK and Ceat  account for
88% of sales.  Bus and Truck tyres account for 65% of production.  The tyre industry has been growing at the rate of 11% per annum. 
The total export of tyres during 2006-07 was 54.49 lakh  an increase by 1.15% over previous year.
 
2.         The Committee was informed about the SWOT analysis of the domestic tyre industry as under:-
 
Strength:
 
1. Availability of qualified manpower and technical professionals
2. Domestic demand can be fully met from the domestic supplies
3. Export of tyres from India has increased acceptance in the world market
4. Competitive domestic market with multiple brands
5. Indian tyres conform to product and safety standards
 
Weaknesses
 
6. Lower spending on basic R&D in comparison to global tyre majors
7. Lower productivity of labour in comparison to world standards.
8. Infrastructural and related bottlenecks.
9. Higher cost of raw-materials.
 
Opportunities
 
10. Robust growth in economy and automobile industry.
11. More export opportunities.

TWENTY-FIRST REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
Having been authorised by the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Industry, I, Ashok Mitra, hereby present the Twenty-first Report of the Committee. 
At the mid point of the fiscal year 1996-97 widespread misgivings were being expressed 
on the uncertain state of industrial growth in the country. The rates of growth of mining, 
power generation and other infrastructure industries were significantly lower compared to 
what these were in the corresponding months of the previous year; the rate of growth of 
manufacturing too was below expectations. Stock exchanges were marked by strong bearish 
sentiments, and there was few evidence of fresh investment activity. At its meeting on 
October 29, 1996 the Committee felt that it would be useful to have a wide-scale survey 
undertaken on its behalf to examine in depth the underlying factors inhibiting industrial 
growth. It was further decided that to facilitate the survey, five Sub-Committees be 
constituted which will assume responsibility for different areas of study. One Sub-Committee 
proposed to analyse the factors inhibiting industrial groups while two other Sub-Committees 
were assigned to concentrate on the problems which directly pertain to the activities of the 
Ministry of Industry, while two other Sub-Committees were assigned to cover the area of 
functioning of the Ministry of Steel and Ministry of Mines respectively. 
The reports finalised by the five Sub-Committees .are placed below. The purpose of this 
brief introduction is to draw attention to some of the more salient conclusions reached by 
the Sub-Committees at the end of their labour. Each Sub-Committee thought it useful to 
visit important metropolitan cities as well as several interior centres of the country in order 
to gain insight at first hand into the problems encountered in the different spheres of 
industrial activity, both organised and non-organised. 
Sub-Committee-III studied at some length the factors which explain the slowing down of 
industrial growth in the current year compared to the trends obtained in 1995-96. While 
arriving at its conclusions, the Sub-Committee has taken into account the generally 
depressed state of industrial growth in the years 1991-92, 1992-93 and 1993-94 as well. 
According to the Sub-Committee, the drying up of the process of investment in the different 
sectors of the economy needs to be reversed as early as possible. lnfrastructural growth in

REPORT 
 
 
 The Department of Public Enterprises (of the Ministry of Heavy Industries and 
Public Enterprises) is the nodal department for all Central Public Sector Enterprises

Authorised by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry , 
I, Ashok Mitra, hereby present the Twenty-second Report of the Committee on the 
Demands for Grants for 1997-98 of the Ministries of Industry, Steel and Mines. 
2. The background of this joint report on the Demands for Grants of the three 
Ministries calls for some explanation. FoUowing the adjournment of Parliament on the 
conclusion of the general discussion of the budget proposals far 1997-98 on March 21, 1997, 
the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Comminees were expected to avail of the 
period till April 21 to prepare and submit their reports on the Demands for Grants of the 
different Ministries alongwith the usual appraisal of the performance budgets for 1996-97 of 
each Ministry. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry 
accordingly met and examined witnesses on March 31, April1, April 2, April 3, April 7 and 
April 8, 1997. (See Appendix). The Standing Committee had scheduled meetings for April 
11, 15 and 17 to discuss the draft reportS on the Demands for Grants. However , these 
meetings had to be postponed because of political developments, including the non-passage 
of the vote of confidence in the Government in the Lok Sabha. In view of the directive of 
the President to the Prime Minister, Parliament is being reconvened on April 21 at 
11.00 a.m. Whether the business placed before Parliament on this date would be confined to 
the passing of a vote on account or whether more substantive issues arc proposed to be 
taken up is not yet known; the constitutional issues involved arc also not altogether clear. 
3. In this circumstance, the Standing Committee has chosen to present to Parliament a 
brief joint report on the activities and proposed Demands for Grants of the three Ministries, 
namely, the Ministry of Mines, the Ministry of Steel and the Ministry of Industry. 
4. The Standing Committee is perturbed at the persistent signs of a slackening in the 
rate of growth in industrial production in recent months. The depressed condition, it was 
initially thought, was a feature of only infrastructural industries such as power and mining. 
Developments in the second quarter of 1996-97 suggest that the malaise is much more 
widespread, and recession appears to be enveloping the capital and consumer goods sectors 
as well, including consumer durables. The growth in the small scale segments of industry is 
assumed to have been over this period somewhat higher than in the organised sector. But

When India began its long and arduous journey towards industrialisation to foster balanced
economic development, Fabian socialism was adopted as the guiding principle. Pandit Nehru’s
vision was to make India an economic powerhouse with the state owned industrial sector as its
backbone. He considered public sector undertakings as “engines of economic growth.” The
emergence of public sector was expected to play a pivotal role in the economic and industrial
development in the country. India’s economy was then primarily an agrarian economy with a weak
industrial base, low level of savings, inadequate investments and lack of infrastructure facilities. As
such, State’s intervention in all the sectors of the economy was inevitable since private sector
neither had necessary resources, the managerial and scientific skill, nor the will to undertake risks
associated with large long-gestation investments. Considering the gaping inequalities that existed in
the economic and social development, it became a pragmatic compulsion to use the public sector
as an instrument for self-reliant economic growth.

buoyancy and dynamism of economic growth and its inclusiveness greatly depend on vibrant and
competitive micro, small and medium enterprises. In fact, some of the developed countries of the
world such as Japan and Switzerland owe their phenomenal economic success to robust medium
and small enterprises which not only provide employment opportunities to vast sections of
population but also significantly boost their exports.

demonstrated when a separate Ministry for dealing with such enterprises was created in the year

at the heart of equitable and inclusive development of economy, the Government has taken several

views of representatives of Central trade unions in the same context.

industry in the recent past has not been satisfactory and that the domestic steel industry has 
been in doldrums for more than a year.

trade unions like CITU and INTUC apprised the Committee that the reasons for the dismal 
performance in the steel industry is due to slowdown in the economy , significant increase in 
input cost, increase in competitiveness in the global market, South-East Asian crisis, decline 
in sales-realisation, reduction of import duty on raw-materials and dumping of steel in India 
by the CIS countries. 
The development and growth of steel . sector is a pre-condition not only for "basic­
industrialisation" but indispensab le for rapid and balanced growth of industrial economy as 
whole. As a matter of fact, steel industry is the backbone of Indian economy as it not only 
provides materials for the "Super structure" in the industrial seCtor but also supplements 
tools and techniques to agriculture sector as well.

having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred and Thirty-fourth

and representatives of select CPSEs & Associations in Auto sector like ACMA, SIAM, FICCI,

1
REPORT
The Department of Heavy Industry deals with many PSEs in the engineering, power and
heavy industry sectors which are critical for nation-building, industrialisation and economic growth.
It also deals with the auto industry which is booming and which has got a lot of potential. Broadly,
the PSEs falling within the following sectors are under the jurisdiction of the Department:–
(i) Heavy Engineering Equipment & Machine Tool Industry (Capital Good Sector);
(ii) H eavy Electrical Engineering Industry; and
(iii) Auto Industry including Tractors and Earth Moving Equipments.
2. DHI aims at ensuring steady growth of all the three above sectors and sub sectors of the
Industry and assists the PSEs in their endeavours to bolster capacity utilization and profitability and
generate resources and reposition their strategies/policies to make them more competitive. The
Department also acts as an interface between PSEs and other agencies for the purpose of long term
policy formulation.

REPORT  
 
The strength of any economy is best reflected in the strength and dynamism of the 
medium, small and micro enterprises.  In our own country, these enterprises constitute the 
mainstay of the architecture of our ec onomy.  These are n ecessary to provide 
employment opportunities to large segments of our population living in far corners of our 
country.  In strengthening and promoting the MSMEs, the culture of inclusive growth is 
promoted.  The significance of the MSMEs can be realized by th e fact that 8 per cent of  
our GDP come from the MSMEs sector.    However, if we look at the percentage share of 
the MSMEs in countries like U.S.A., U.K. and Ch ina, it comes to 40 to 60 per cent.  This 
means that in our country, we have not been able to harness the potential of the MSME 
sector.   
 
2. In the documents supplied to the Committee, it is stated that the vision for 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterp rises is to ensure an orderly and robust 
growth and development of Micr o, Small and Medium Enterpri ses so that these could be 
strengthened to accelerate our economic growth.

Nagaland State is a classic case of a state owned c ompany which became a 
non-starter from its very inception.  The founders of this company 
articulated a bold, forward looking and lofty visio n by stating that it would 
be the market leader in the manufacture of world cl ass eco-friendly paper by 
adopting innovative technologies for sustainable development and to strike a 
harmonious relationship between nature and industry .  Established as a joint 
venture company of the Government of Nagaland and H industan Paper 
Corporation Limited (A Government of India Enterprise) it was incorporated 
on 14 th  September 1971 for production of pulp and paper by  using abundant 
bamboo of the north-eastern region.

increase in the cost of construction of the project  was indicative of the 
problem of cost overruns which plagued the company and became awe of

Industry, having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred 
and Fiftieth Report on impact of Foreign Direct Inv estment (FDI) in retail on MSME 
sector pertaining to Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
 
2.  The Committee heard the representatives of Mini stry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises, Department of Industrial Policy  & Promotion. The Committee also 
sought the views of public through Press-Release an d heard representatives of select 
industry associations/experts on the issue.  
 
3.  The Committee in its meeting held on 22

New Delhi,  
July, 2013 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(ii) 
 
 
 
 
 
 

REPORT  
 
 
            Foreign investment denotes investment made by a non-resident entity 
in an enterprise in the host country. This can happ en through FDI (Foreign 
Direct Investment) and  Foreign Portfolio Investmen t by FIIs (Foreign 
Institutional Investors) or private equity funds et c.  The FDI denotes foreign 
capital with a longer term perspective and often in vested in productive 
enterprise and may seek managerial control over ent erprise.  Of many other 
modes of getting external finance, FDI is preferred mode due to its long term 
stable nature.  It is less volatile  and does not g enerate or add to debt  
liabilities for the host country. 
 
2. In order to discount unwarranted implications, i n India the FDI flow is 
allowed either through Government route or automatic route. The sectors not 
included in automatic route need Government's appro val and proposals are 
considered by inter-ministerial Foreign Investment Promotion Board under 
M/o Finance or Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion 
(DIPP).  Sectors in which FDI is prohibited include  lottery, chit fund, 
gambling/betting, agriculture and plantation

REPORT  
 
BACKGROUND 
 
The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) is a statutory 
body established by an Act of Parliament, 1956, In April 1957, it took over the 
work of former All India Khadi and Village Industries Board. It functions under 
the administrative control of Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
 
2. The statement of objects and reasons of the orig inal KVIC Act, 1956 
states that "with a view to promoting and developing Khadi and Village 
Industries, the Central Govt. constituted a Board called the All India Khadi and 
Village Industries Board and vested it with powers to prepare and organize 
programmes for the production and development of Kh adi and Village 
Industries and to deal with other matters incidenta l thereto.  It has, however, 
been found in actual practice that the work of the 'Board' has been hampered 
by certain procedural and financial difficulties, w hich would be removed if a 
Commission were set up by law.  It is, therefore, p roposed to set up a 
Commission, called All India Khadi and Village Indu stries Commission which 
will be vested with the powers, executive as well a s administrative, for the 
proper development of Khadi and Village Industries.   The bill also provide for 
the All India Khadi and V.I. Board functioning as a n advisory body which will 
advise the Commission generally in the discharge of its duties. “

been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred Ninety Report on the Professionalization
of Boards of CPSEs pertaining to the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises (Department of

over a series of meetings, the Committee heard the views of Secretaries of Department of Public Enterprises
(DPE), Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), representatives of Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB),
Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) and
Institute of Company Secretaries of India (ICSI) and also had interactions with certain CPSEs.

Members during the meetings of the Committee and to the questionnaire sent by the Secretariat.
4. I, thank DPE, MCA, PESB, SEBI, ICAI, ICSI and various CPSEs for furnishing inputs during the
meetings and thereafter.

THIRD REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman, Department- Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, 
having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this 
Third Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants for 1993-94 of the Ministry of 
Mines. 
2. In pursuance of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Rajya Sabha 
pertaining to Department-Related Standing Committees, Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha 
and Hon'ble Speaker , Lok Sabha nominated 42 members of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha to 
the Committee on Industry for the functions assigned to it under the Rules. Further 
Chairman, Rajya Sabha and Speaker, Lok Sabha decided that all provisions of Rule 270 of 
the Rules relating to the functions of the Committee shall become operative with effect from 
30th March, 1993. 
3. The Committee on Industry deals with the subjects falling in the jurisdiction of the 
Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Steel and Ministry of Mines. 
4. The Committee accordingly held its first meeting on the 22nd April, 1993 and 
considered relevant documents and papers received from the Ministry of Mines on the 
Demands for Grants for the year 1993-94. 
5. The Committee also heard the oral evidence of the Secretary of the Ministry of Mines 
on the performance budget in the context of Demands for Grants of that Ministry. 
6. The Committee considered the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in three sittings and 
considered and adopted the Report at its sitting held on 4th May, 1993 (Annexure consisting 
of the minutes of the First, Fourth and Fifth sittings of the Committee). 
7. Demands for Grants as presented for the Ministry as under:-

Total Voted 209.41 crores

of the Ministry and the other documents. The Committee is conscious of the fact that the 
Demands for Grants of various Ministries and Departments are to be put for vote of the 
Lok Sabha on the 4th May, 1993. We, therefore, offer general comments. We propose to 
consider the detailed expenditure at a later stage and will present our views in subsequent 
reports so as to enable the Government to recaste their expenditure priorities in the revised 
estimates.

on Industry, having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this T hree 
Hundred and Fourth Report on Demands for Grants (20 21-22) pertaining to the 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises.

questionnaires, Annual Report of the Ministry, Notes on Demands and other 
background papers provided by the Ministry.  The Committee heard the views of the 
Secretary and officers from KVIC, Coir Board and SIDBI during the meeting. The 
Committee also invited the written views /suggestions of some of the prominent 
MSME Associations and incorporated some meaningful suggestions in the Report.

THIRTY -SECOND REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry 
ha.ving been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this 
Thirty-second Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of 
Indusrry for 1999-2000. 
While examining the said Demands for Grants, the Committee also considered the 
Action Taken Notes of Ministry of Industry on its 25th Report pertaining to the Demands 
for Grants of Ministry of Industry for 1998-99. The Committee examined the relevant 
documents and papers relating to the Demands for GrantS for 1999-2000 received from the 
Ministry of Industry and beard the oral evidence of Secretaries of Ministry of Industry in this 
connection. The Committee also held discussions with the representatives of Cll, F1CCI, 
ASSOCHAM, PHD Chamber of Commerce, Laghu Udyog Bharati, Disinvestment 
Commission and SCOPE. 
The Committee adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 16th April, 1999. 
The comments and observations with suitable recommendarions of the Committee are 
given in the succeeding paragraphs: 
1. The activities of Department of Industri al Development relate to the promotion of 
industrialisation encompassing the development of medium as well as large industries in 
public and private sectors, revival, restr ucturing, research & development, grant of patents, 
registration of trade marks, designs, productivity and quality measures. A sum of Rs. 361.59 
crore (plan Rs. 342.77 crore & non-plan Rs. 18.52 crore) was allocated to it for its total 
expenditure in the budget estimate 1998-99 and it was enhanced to Rs. 443.25 crore (plan 
Rs. 420.60 & non-plan Rs. 22.65 crore) in the revised estimate. The Committee, while 
examining the Demands for Grants (1999-2000) of the Department, had the opportunity to 
have an overview of the activities undertak en by institutions under this Department. 
2. The National Productivity Council (NPC) is an autonomous organisation under the 
administrative control of this Department. It has the objectives of generating productivity 
consciousness and providing productivity services to various sectors of national economy. 
The NPC was provided Rs. 7.44 crore in the BE 1998-99 which was reduced to Rs. 2.00 
crore in RE 1998-99. The Committee was informed that the reduction at the RE stage took

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Three Hundred 
Twenty-Fourth Report on the subject Promotion of Electric Vehicles in the Country. 
 2.  The Committee took up the subject for detailed examination. As part of 
examination of the subject, the Committee deliberated in detail in its meetings held on 
10th January & 23rd June, 2023, wherein it heard the views of  the Ministry of Heavy 
Industries, Ministry of Power, Ministry of Road, Transport & Highway,  Ministry of 
Petroleum & Natural Gas, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, 
Ministry of New & Renewable Energy, Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue), 
NITI Aayog,  SMEV and during its study visit to various leading EV Manufacturers of 
the Country.  
3.  The Report is based on the submissions made by the Secretaries  & Officers of 
various Ministries; representatives of SMEV and EV Manufacturers; and other materials 
such as Background Notes, Power-Point Presentations and replies to the questionnaires 
submitted to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in 
connection with the examination of the subject.

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Three Hundred 
Twenty-Eighth Report on the subject Review of Performance of Prime Minister's 
Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP).

examination of the subject, the Committee deliberated in detail and,  
 
i. Reviewed background data and annual reports of the ministry, its official website to 
identify challenges or areas for improvement 
ii. Interacted with officials from the Ministry, key stakeholders like KVIC, public 
sector banks, and beneficiaries 
iii. Circulated detailed questions. 
iv. Conducted study visits to Udaipur (Rajasthan), Mumbai (Maharashtra), Goa, 
Vishakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Kolkata (West Bengal), Srinagar (Jammu

Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), for placing their valuable suggestions in 
connection with examination of the subject before the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry.

FOURTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, 
present this Fourth Report of the Committee on the status of Mini Steel Plants. 
2. The Committee on Industry deals with the subjects falling within the jurisdiction of 
the Ministries of Industry, Steel and Mines. 
3. The Committee at its meeting held on 15th June, 1993 identified 'Mini Steel Plants -
their status' as one of the subjects relating to the Ministry of Steel for its indepth study and 
report. The Committee directed the Secretariat to obtain a note on the subject for its 
consideration. 
4. The Committee held a general discussion on the existing status of Mini Steel Plants in 
the country on Monday, the 28th June, 1993 in the light of the note furnished by the 
Ministry. The Committee finalised a questionnaire for further clarifications by the Ministry 
on the subject. 
5. The Committee also heard the oral evidence of the Secretary of the Ministry on the 
subject on the 29th September, 1993. 
6. The Committee considered the subject in three sittings and considered and adopted 
the Report at its sitting held on 20th December, 1993.

Steel Plant" generally refers to electric arc furnac e unit where melting scrap is reheated and 
refined to produce steel ingots/billets. During the seventies in view of the indigenous 
availability of steel melting scrap , units were allowed to produce mild steel ignots to meet 
the demand of structural steel for construction purposes. At present, there are 177 Mini

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Forty-Second Report 
on the coal India (Regulation ofTransfers and Validation) Bill, 1995. 
2. The Coal India (Regulation of Transfers and Validation) Bill, 1995 was introduced in 
Rajya Sabha on the 141h February, 1995 and was referred * to the Committee on Industry by the 
Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 2nd February, 2000 under Rule 270 (b) of the Rules of 
procedure and Conduct of Business in Rajya Sabha for examination and report thereon. 
3. The Committee in its meeting held on 15th May, 2000 took oral evidence of Secretary of 
Ministry of Coal and Joint Secretary & Legislative Counsel of Ministry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs ( Legislative Department). In Order to take stock of legal issues involved in the 
Bill, the Committee again heard Joint Secretary & Legislative Counsel of the Ministry of Law, 
Justice and Company Affairs on 25th May, 2000. For further clarification, the Committee heard 
the .Secretary ofMinistry of Coal and Ministry Law, Justice and Company Affairs (Legislative 
Department) on 22nd June, 2000. The Committee also took up the clause-by-clause consideration 
of the Bill in the said meeting. 
4. The Committee wishes to thank the representatives of the Ministry of Coal and 
Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs ( Legislative Department) for appearing before the 
Committee for oral evidence and placing their considered views before the Committee. The 
Committee also wishes to thank the Ministry of Coal and the Ministry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs (Legislative Department) for furnishing the replies to the questionnaire and the 
points raised during the course of oral evidence. 
5. The Committee considered and adopted the report on the Bill in its meeting held on 19th 
July, 2000. 
6. A note of dissent given by Shri Jibon Roy, M.P. and Shri Sunil Khan, M.P. is appended 
to the report as Annexure-!.

L the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry. having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Forty-third Report on 
the Credit Flow to Small scale Industries. Taking into account the significance of Small Scale 
Sector it was decided in the Committee's meeting held on 25th September, 2000 that the 
Committee should assess the Credit Flow to the Sector in the aftermath of the policy announced 
by the Hon'ble Prime Minister in the First National Conference of SSI Sector on the 30th August, 
2000. 
2. The Committee at its meeting held on 25th September, 2000, inter-alia examined the 
background note on the Credit Flow to SSI sector furnished by the Ministry of SSI and A&RI 
and thereafter, decided to have interaction with officials of the Ministry of Small Scale 
Industries and Agro & Rural Industries, RBI!Banks/Financial Institutions/KVIC and 
representatives of SSI Association and NGOs to assess the impact of the policy/package on the 
SSI units. 
3. The Committee in its next meeting held on 4th October, 2000 decided to undertake a 
visit to Mumbai from gth to II th October, 2000 to take stock of the ground realities pertaining to 
credit facilities being extended to SSI sector by the Banks and Financial Institutions. 
4. The Report has been prepared on the basis of the background note furnished by the 
Ministry of SSI and A&RI and discussions held in three days meeting in Mumbai with the 
representatives of SSI and NGO and officials the Ministry of SSI and A&RI and RBI/Banks 
and Financial Institutions. On behalf of the Committee I wish to thank all the representatives and 
officials who appeared before the Committee and·· placed their considered views. The 
Committee, while appreciating the concern of the Government to SSI Sector, hopes that the 
Government will implement the recommendations made in the present report in order to ensure 
the continued credit flow to SSI sector. 
5. The Committee in its meeting held on 18th December, 2000 considered and adopted 
the Report.

I.          INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1       The Department of Heavy Industry is concerned with the development of the heavy engineering industry,
machine tool industry, heavy electrical industry, industrial machinery and auto-industry. The Industries covered by this
Department provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport.
They also cater to the requirements of equipments for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers,
refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, textiles, paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for development of
a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gear boxes.
It is  also  vested with the administrative charge of 48 Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).
 
1.2       The  PSEs under the administrative control of the Department are engaged in manufacturing of

1.1       The Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries (SSI & ARI) is the nodal ministry for policy
formulation, promotion, development and protection of small scale industries. It also monitors the implementation of
these policies.
 
1.2       Ministry of SSI & ARI designs  and implements the policies through its field organizations for promotion and
growth of small and tiny enterprises, including the coir industries. The Ministry also coordinates with other
Ministries/Departments on behalf the Small Scale Industries (SSI) sector.
 
1.3       Implementation of   policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services
to small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organisation
(SIDO), statutory bodies/other organizations like Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) and Coir Board; a
Public Sector Undertaking – National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC); and three training institutes – National
Institute of Small Industry Extension Training  (NISIET), Hyderabad; National Institute for Entrepreneurship and Small
Business Development (NIESBUD), New Delhi and Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship (IIE), Guwahati.

2. The Committee in its sitting held on 28th June , 1993 considered a note receiv ed from the 
Ministry of Steel on Sponge Iron and decjded to send a questionnaire to the Ministr y on the 
subject for their replies. In its sitting held on 29th September , 1993, the Committe e heard the 
views of the Secretary of the Ministry of Steel by way of clarifications to the repl ies sent by the 
Ministry to the said questionnaire. 
3. The Committee considered in depth the problems prevailing in sponge iron industr y and 
Government's efforts to protect its interests. The Committee had deliberations on the overall 
present scenario with a view to project the possible ways in salvaging the sponge Iron Indust ries. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the report at its sitting held on the lOth February. 
1994. 
5. Based on the papers and other relevant material on the subject and also the evidence of 
the Secretary, the Committee had noted the following picture of the Sponge Iron indu stry in the 
country. 
5.1 Sponge iron is a partial substitute for steel melting Scrap. It is a met allic product 
produced by direct induction of high grade iron ore or pellets in the solid stat e i.e. without the 
material going into the liquid phase as in the blast furnace. It is also known as Direct Reduced 
Iron (DRI) or Hot Briquetted Iron (HBI). This reduction of iron ore can be achieved by using 
either carbon bearing material such as non-coking coal or a suitable redu cing gas produced by 
reforming of natural gas. On the other hand sponge iron can also be used in the integrated steel 
plants to replace steel melting scrap to some extent as a coolant in the LD convertors and as a 
part of the change mix in the basic oxygen furnace and open hearth furnace. 
5.2 Non-coking coal and natural gas are the two main ingredients in spong e iron technology. 
Earlier the technology was limited upto use. of non-coking coal but with the technological 
innovation gas based sponge iron plants have also been set up. While coal based technology 
involves reduction of iron ore in a rotary kiln using non-coking coal as a reduct ant, gas based one 
uses Hydrogen or Carbon Mono Oxide or a mixture of both as reductant s. Gas based sponge iron 
manufacturing process requires high-grade iron ore with around 65%. At present non-coking coal 
is imported for sponge iron industry. Less availability of high grade of iron ore and Jack of

a detailed Background Note on the subject from the Ministry of Mines. 
3. At its sitting held on 28th June, 1993 the Committee held a general discussion on the 
note furnished by the Ministry on the subject and finalised a questionnaire for furth er 
clarificatiOns by the Ministry. 
4. The Committee also heard the oral ev1aence of the Secretary of the Ministry alongwith 
the representat ives of Bharat Gold Mines Limited at its two meetings held on 30th September

5. The Committee at its meeting held on the 9th November, 1993 also heard the oral

The Industries covered by this Department provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport. They also cater to the requirements of equipment for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, textiles, paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for the development of a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gearboxes. 1          Agro and Rural Industries play an important role in the economy of our country. This sector  has vast potential in
terms of employment and dispersal of industries in rural areas. In view of its growing importance, the Ministry of Agro
& Rural Industries  was carved out of the erstwhile Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries  
w.e.f. 1st September, 2001. The main function of the Ministry is to formulate policy measures for the growth of rural
industries for achieving rapid increase in gainful employment and balanced regional growth  which are among the main
objectives underlying the strategy of industrialization in the country. It also supervises and coordinates the activities of
different promotional agencies operating at the Central and State Level.

by the Committee, hereby present this Ninetieth Report on Sickness in SSI Sector in the city of Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh.

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER

REPORT
BACKGROUND
          Situated on the banks of the river Ganga, Kanpur stands as one of North India's major industrial centres with its
own historical, religious and commercial importance. The city, which was once described as Manchester of the East, is
one of the biggest producers of textile and leather products in Uttar Pradesh. These are exported in bulk from here.
About 50 tonnes of air cargo is generated from leather products only. Apart from leather and textile industries, fertilizer,
chemicals, two wheelers, soaps, pan masala, hosiery and engineering industries are also operating in the city.
1.1     The city hosts the world famous Lal Imli woollen factory, which was once the pride of the State. Besides, many
big companies such as LML Ltd., Kothari Products, Coca Cola, Pepsi, Duncans Industries Ltd. (Fertilizer factory),
Rotomac, Nerolac, Hindustan Lever, Ashok Masale, Goldie Spices, Mirza Tanners, Super House, BIC, NTC, GCMMF
(Amul) etc. have their offices/plants at Kanpur. The stockyards of HAL and SAIL are also located in the city. A large
number of ordnance factories and defence establishments such as DMSRDE, Small Arms Factory, Field Gun Factory
and Parachute Factory are also located in Kanpur. Gas Authority of India Ltd., NTPC, and perfume industries of
Kannauj are very close to Kanpur. A Software Technology Park is also being developed here. The city also hosts the
offices of the Directorate of Industries and Directorate of Handloom to look after these industries.

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER

COIR INDUSTRY -AN OVERVIEW
 
1.0     Coconut cultivation in India is concentrated in Kerala, which accounts for 48.63 per cent of the total production. Historically, the coir
industry took root in Kerala because of the availability of skilled labour and natural facilities of retting of coconut husk.
 
1.1     The development of the coir industry has been in areas where there is concentration of coconut cultivation and availability of coconut husk.
The coir industry is of great importance to Kerala, where it is second only to agriculture as a source of employment. With the expansion of
coconut cultivation and the concerted efforts of the Coir Board and the respective State Governments, the coir industry is coming up in Tamil
Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal and Assam. Kerala is the largest producer of coconuts and its contribution is as much as
50.5 per cent of total production.
 
1.2     Indian coir is exquisite live-in style, hygiene products of traditional and modern design consisting of handmade and machinemade
materials. It is helping a million disadvantaged women to earn their livelihood. Coconut husk is a natural product from a renewable source.

INTRODUCTION
1. The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is an agreement between the Government, being the owner, and specific PSE. The
obligations and mutual responsibilities of both the parties are clearly specified indicating the intensions and the objectives to be achieved.
The main objectives of the MoU system were to improve the performance of the PSE through enhanced autonomy and accountability. It
was also envisaged through the system to provide clarity of goals and objectives to be achieved.

Committee at its various meetings deliberated upon the MoU system as a performance improvement instrument and examined the
